name: Budha Subba Temple
deity: Budha Subba (deified spirit of Buddhi Karna Raya Khebang Limbu)
significance: A shrine at Bijayapur near Dharan venerating the spirit of Buddhi Karna Raya Khebang Limbu, the last Limbu king, who was killed in 1773; local Limbu people began worshipping his wandering soul at his tomb as an old king, and he is honoured as a protective deity.
story: Shiva and Parvati are said to have come to Vijayapur in disguise on a hunt, planted their bows in the ground and sat in penance, vanishing when they sensed the approach of Kali Yuga, while bamboo sprouted from the bows they left behind.

name: Bala Tripura Sundari Temple
deity: Durga as Bala Tripura Sundari Bhagawati
builtDisplay: est. 1057 CE; said to be 12th c.
significance: A goddess temple on the bank of the Thuli Bheri river near Tripurakot in Dolpa District, dedicated to Durga in her Bala Tripura Sundari form and traditionally dated to the 11th-12th century.
story: King Bikram Shahi is said to have uncovered an image of Bhagwati in an excavated pit, from which butterflies flew out and turned to stone, one of them marking the spot where the temple was raised.

name: Tal Barahi Temple
significance: A two-storey stone pagoda on a small island in Phewa Lake at Pokhara, dedicated to the goddess Barahi and reachable only by boat; pilgrims come chiefly in Baisakh and Kartik and during Dashain.

name: Siddha Baba Temple
significance: A Shiva shrine on the left bank of the Tinau river at Dobhan, about two kilometres from Butwal, whose precincts also hold images of Ganesh, Nag, Mansa Devi and Bishwokarma; it was registered with the Palpa district administration in 1998.
story: The site is held to be where King Bhartrihari, elder brother of Vikramaditya, performed his penance.

name: Sankata Temple
deity: Sankata (identified by Buddhists with Chanda Maharoshan)
builtDisplay: dating unrecorded; founded by King Gunakama Dev
significance: A shrine at Te Bahal in central Kathmandu, credited to King Gunakama Dev, whose deity is petitioned to turn away misfortune and sickness; Hindus worship the goddess as Sankata while Buddhists identify the image with Chanda Maharoshan.
story: A Bajracharya guru named Bandhu Ratna is said to have used tantric power to confine Sankata and a Yogini inside holy pitchers, which were then enshrined in the temple built for them.

name: Palanchok Bhagawati Temple
significance: A pagoda temple on the summit of Palanchok hill in Kavrepalanchok District, some 42 km from Kathmandu, enshrining an eighteen-armed image of Bhagawati revered as a protector against danger and misfortune; it is believed to have been raised during the reign of King Manadeva in the fifth century.
story: She is held to be the elder sister of all the other Bhagawati goddesses of Nepal.

name: Venkatesh Mandir, Kathmandu
significance: A Vaishnava temple at Battisputali in Kathmandu founded in 1898, after the devotee Garudhwaj Ramanuja Dasi and her husband Govindacharya brought an image of Balaji home from the Tirumala Venkateswara temple in India.

name: Dolakha Bhimsen Temple
deity: Bhimsen (Bhindyo), worshipped as god of trade and fortune
significance: A shrine in Bhimeshwar, about 4.5 km east of Charikot in Dolakha District, where Bhimsen is worshipped as the god of trade, commerce and fortune; its founding date is unknown, but an inscription of 1611 records a renovation.
story: Porters cooking rice beside the shrine are said to have realised that a triangular black stone was Bhimsen himself when the rice touching it stayed raw, and the stone bled milk mixed with blood when struck.

name: Dakneshwori Temple
place: Pato Bazaar, Dakneshwori Municipality, Saptari District
significance: A pagoda-style goddess temple at Pato Bazaar in Dakneshwori Municipality of Saptari District, dedicated to Dakneshwori Bhagawati; the municipality takes its name from the shrine, whose present structure was reconstructed in the 1990s.

name: Balkumari Temple, Lalitpur
deity: Balkumari, one of the Ashtamatrika mother goddesses
significance: A pagoda shrine at Tyagal in Lalitpur (Patan) dedicated to Balkumari, counted among the Ashtamatrika mother goddesses; its origin is disputed, with estimates placing it anywhere between the 7th and the 17th century.
story: The original image was stolen twice, and on one occasion the aeroplane it had been loaded onto at Tribhuvan International Airport could not take off, so the idol was recovered and returned to the shrine.

name: Jal Binayak Temple
significance: The foremost Ganesh shrine of the Chobhar area south of Kathmandu, first raised in Nepal Sambat 723 by the Malla king Shiva Singh; Sri Nivas Malla of Patan added its finial in 789 NS and Rajya Prakash Malla of Kathmandu rebuilt the present pagoda in 871 NS.

name: Daunne Devi Temple
significance: A wayside shrine on the Daunne pass at Dumkibas in Bardaghat, Nawalparasi District, holding both a Durga shrine and a Shivalaya; its founding is attributed to Jung Bahadur Rana, while the present building dates from 2055 BS and has been looked after by the local user committee since 2049 BS.
story: The Daunne hill was known in ancient times as Trikut Parbat and is held to have been a place of meditation for the sage Valmiki and for Mayadevi, the mother of the Buddha.

name: Balkumari Temple, Thimi
significance: A seventeenth-century pagoda at Thimi in Bhaktapur District dedicated to the goddess Balkumari and counted among the four Kumari temples of the Kathmandu Valley; a Bhairab shrine stands in the same courtyard, and the Sindoor Jatra is celebrated here at Nepali New Year.
story: A merchant of Thimi is said to have won a princess of Lubhu who would come with him only if the goddess Balkumari came too, and so the goddess moved from Lubhu to Thimi.

name: Dungeshwor Temple
place: Naule Katuwal, Dullu Municipality, Dailekh District
significance: A pagoda-style Shiva temple at Naule Katuwal in Dullu Municipality of Dailekh District, worshipped as Sidheshwor Mahadev and sharing its precinct with shrines to Kalika Bhagwati, Ganesh, Kalsaini Bhairab and Batuk Bhairab; the article records that the saint Sagar Giri organised its worship and that its ritual regalia were restored in 1960 BS.

name: Chandannath Temple
place: Khalanga Bazar, Chandannath Municipality, Jumla District
significance: The chief temple of Jumla, standing above Khalanga Bazar in Chandannath Municipality and dedicated to Dattatreya; it was raised under the Kalyal dynasty, of whose rule and of whose connection with Chandannath few written records survive.
story: Chandannath Baba is said to have carried an image of Dattatreya here from Kashmir, and a cow that gave up her milk of her own accord on the spot is said to have revealed the sacred ground on which the temple was then built.

name: Rajarshi Janak Mandir
significance: A temple at Janak Chowk in Janakpur, Dhanusha District, dedicated to Rajarshi Janak, the Vedic king of Videha after whom the city is named; it stands in the Mithila region among other shrines tied to the Ramayana.

name: Bhairabsthan Temple
builtDisplay: dating unrecorded; founded by King Mukunda Sen
significance: A hilltop Bhairab temple about 9 km northwest of Tansen in Palpa District, at roughly 1,470 m, established by King Mukunda Sen of the Sena dynasty during the period when Palpa was his capital.
story: Mukunda Sen is said to have carried off an image of Bhairav from the Matsyendranath temple during his attack on Kathmandu and to have installed it here in Palpa.

name: Satyawati Temple
significance: A goddess shrine beside a hill lake at Satyawati in Palpa District, about 30 km south of Tansen and 19 km north of Butwal, revered by the Magar community as their own deity and reached on a foot trail from the Jhumsa bridge on the Siddhartha Highway.
story: On the night of the festival the goddess is said to grant the wishes of pilgrims who walk three times round the lake and call their wish aloud.

name: Gokarneshwor Mahadev Temple
place: Gokarna, northeast of Bodhnath, Kathmandu District
significance: A Shiva temple near Gokarna village, northeast of Bodhnath in the Kathmandu Valley, whose sanctum houses a lingam of considerable importance in the valley's Shaiva worship.

name: Maula Kalika Temple
significance: A temple of the goddess Kalika above Gaindakot town in Nawalpur District of Gandaki Province, one of the better-known Shakta shrines of central Nepal.

name: Swargadwari
significance: A hill pilgrimage centre in Pyuthan District dedicated to Narayana and Shiva, established in 1895 (Vaisakha Purnima 1952 BS) by Guru Maharaj Narayana Gautama Khatri, known as Swami Hamsananda, who spent most of his life on the ridge herding and milking thousands of cows; the site is closely bound to the veneration of the cow in Hinduism.

name: Ganeshthan Temple
significance: A Ganesha temple in ward 11 of Bharatpur in Chitwan District whose original shrine is placed in the fifteenth century and credited to Muni Makunda, king of Palpa; the present building went up in 1952 during the reign of King Mahendra, and worshippers gather chiefly on Tuesdays.

name: Kumbheshwar Temple
significance: A five-storey free-standing pagoda dedicated to Shiva, standing about 200 m north of Patan Durbar Square in Lalitpur and built around 1392 by King Jayasthiti Malla.
story: The ponds within the temple courtyard are believed to be fed by a spring rising from Gosainkunda, some 43 km north of Kathmandu.

name: Naradevi Temple
deity: Sweta Kali, called Nyata Ajima by Newars
significance: A shrine in central Kathmandu dedicated to Sweta Kali, known among Newars as Nyata Ajima, and believed to have been founded in the ninth century by Gunakamadeva, the founder of the city; its three-tiered roof includes a gilded storey carried on carved struts.
story: A king of Patan who lost his way while hunting and was chased by a wild elephant is said to have hidden in a tree at this spot, where the goddess Swetakali appeared and gave him back his life, upon which he founded the temple.

name: Bhutandevi Mandir
significance: A pagoda temple in Hetauda, Makwanpur District, dedicated to Bhutandevi, identified with Hidimbi, a wife of Bhima and the mother of Ghatotkacha.
story: Hidimba is held to be another manifestation of Durga, and the name of Hetauda itself is believed to come from the goddess.

name: Bhadrakali Temple, Pokhara
place: Kundahar, east of Pokhara, Kaski District
significance: A hilltop pagoda at Kundahar east of Pokhara in Kaski District, founded in 1817 and dedicated to Bhadrakali as goddess of power and strength; it stands at about 2,930 feet over some 135 ropanies and is reached by stairways of 292 steps from the east and 265 from the south.
story: The goddess is said to have told a priest to dig into the hill, where her image was uncovered and thereafter worshipped as Bhadrakali.

name: Kapileshwar Temple, Janakpur
significance: One of the Shiva shrines that mark the corners of Janakpur in Dhanusha District, worshipped as Kapileshwar Mahadev; raised originally in the Simrangad style, it was rebuilt after the earthquake of 1934.
story: King Janak is said to have built Shiva temples at the four corners of his capital Janakpur in the Treta Yuga, and the sage Kapil to have kept his ashram at this one, which is how it got its name.

name: Bishnupaduka
significance: A shikhara shrine at Dharan in Sunsari District built over a rock bearing two footprints venerated as those of Vishnu.
story: Local people are said to have come upon a rock marked with two clear footprints, which are believed to be Vishnu's own.

name: Manakamana Temple, Sankhuwasabha
significance: A pagoda temple of Manakamana Devi about 5 km north of Tumlingtar airport in Sankhuwasabha District, eastern Nepal, distinct from the better-known Manakamana shrine in Gorkha.
story: A farmer ploughing his field is said to have struck a stone that oozed milk and blood, which the devotee Lakhan Thapa read as the return of a seventeenth-century queen of Gorkha who had committed sati after her husband's death.

name: Sheshnarayan Temple
significance: A pagoda temple of Vishnu in his Sheshnarayan form near Pharping in the southern Kathmandu Valley, believed to have been raised in the reign of the Licchavi king Vishnugupta; it is counted among the four Narayana temples of the valley.
story: The four Narayana temples are said to stand on hilltops at the cardinal points to guard the Kathmandu Valley.

name: Kalika Bhagawati Temple
significance: A pagoda temple southeast of Baglung town on the southern bank of the Kali Gandaki in Gandaki Province, dedicated to Kalika, one of the fiercest forms of Shakti.
story: A king is said to have received the goddess's image as dowry, and when the wedding party halted overnight in a forest and no one could lift the idol the next morning, he built the temple on that spot.

name: Rajdevi Temple, Gaur
significance: A Hindu temple at Gaur in Rautahat District of Madhesh Province whose presiding deity is the goddess Rajdevi; the surrounding municipality takes its name from the shrine.

name: Kulpani Mandir
place: Badahara, Gadhawa Rural Municipality, Dang District
significance: A pagoda-style Shiva temple at Badahara in ward 1 of Gadhawa Rural Municipality, Dang District, Lumbini Province.

name: Chintang Devi Temple
significance: A goddess temple in Dhankuta District dedicated to Chintang Devi, also called Jalpadevi, and held in reverence in both Hindu and Kirati worship.
story: The shrine takes its name from Chintang, one of the seven daughters of Budhahang.

name: Bhaleshwor Mahadev Temple
significance: A pagoda temple of Shiva on the summit of Chandragiri hill on the southwestern rim of the Kathmandu Valley in Bagmati Province.
story: The shrine is said to mark the place where the forehead of Sati Devi fell as Shiva carried her lifeless body across the world after her death at her father's sacrifice.
